overview: The exact atlas id sind is best matched to the Samma Sultanate, a locally rooted Muslim dynasty that ruled much of Sindh from about 1351 until a phased Arghun takeover ending about 1524. From Thatta and earlier Samui, the Jams negotiated Delhi pressure, regional chiefs, Gujarat ties, Indus agriculture, desert edges, and Indian Ocean commerce. Under Jam Nizamuddin, canals, cultivated land, scholarship, stone carving, and Makli patronage flourished, although later chronicles often praise more freely than contemporary evidence permits. Daily life joined farming, fishing, herding, craft, trade, household work, mosque study, Sufi institutions, and river transport. Ordinary families, women, children, medicine, houses, and toilets are poorly recorded, so this card marks what the sources cannot securely say. Written-language sample: السلطان نظام الدين شاه, al-Sultan Nizam al-Din Shah, means Sultan Nizam al-Din Shah; a numismatic study quotes it from his dated tomb inscription. The atlas polygon appears only in 1492, includes sampled Multan, excludes sampled Umerkot, and disappears in 1500 while Samma rule continued. It is a coarse locator, not a surveyed frontier.

periods.title: About 1351 to 1365: Samma power replaces Soomra rule
periods.summary: Jam Unar and related Samma leaders emerged from a longer contest with the Soomras and Delhi governors. Muhammad bin Tughluq died during his 1351 Sindh expedition, easing imperial pressure. The early succession is reconstructed from chronicles written later, so individual reign boundaries remain approximate rather than stopwatch-precise.

periods.title: About 1365 to 1392: Tughluq campaigns, tribute, captivity, and return
periods.summary: Firuz Shah Tughluq campaigned against lower Sindh, endured logistical difficulty, and eventually compelled submission. Samma rulers and families experienced detention, tribute, and divided authority before Jam Tamachi returned. The period shows that independence was negotiated and reversible, not a clean one-day break from Delhi.

periods.title: About 1392 to 1428: succession among the Jams
periods.summary: A sequence of Jams followed Tamachi, including short and disputed reigns that later histories order differently. Coins and inscriptions are scarce, while repeated royal names create confusion. Sindh nevertheless remained a recognizable Samma realm as Delhi weakened after Timur and regional courts gained room to maneuver.

periods.title: About 1428 to 1453: Jam Tughluq and a longer consolidation
periods.summary: Jam Tughluq, also called Jam Juna, receives a comparatively long reign in reconstructed chronologies. Monumental inscriptions at Makli help anchor his identity better than later king lists alone. That combination of texts and stones illustrates how historians repair a dynasty whose administrative archive has largely disappeared.

periods.title: About 1453 to 1461: Jam Sanjar and the road to Nizamuddin
periods.summary: After another unsettled succession, Jam Sanjar ruled before Jam Nizamuddin, remembered as Jam Nindo, took the throne. Regional ties joined chiefs, scholars, Sufi families, and neighboring Gujarat. Precise palace politics remain elusive because much surviving evidence comes from funerary architecture and chronicles produced generations afterward.

periods.title: About 1461 to 1490: Nizamuddins long reign and Thatta patronage
periods.summary: Jam Nizamuddin ruled for nearly five decades. Thatta and Makli became linked centers of government, learning, devotion, craft, and burial, while irrigation and cultivation supported the realm. UNESCO dates his reign from 1461 to 1509; other scholarship gives 1508, a small but real chronological disagreement.

periods.title: About 1490 to 1508: frontier defense and the height of Makli craft
periods.summary: Arghun forces pressing from the northwest tested the later Nizamuddin state. Darya Khan became an important commander and administrator, while masons and carvers created the rulers unfinished but richly ornamented tomb. The late reign combined military strain with durable investment in water, learning, and monumental memory.

periods.title: About 1508 to 1524: Jam Firuz, civil rivalry, and Arghun takeover
periods.summary: After Nizamuddins death, young Jam Firuz faced rival Jam Salah al-Din and weakening elite support. Shah Beg Arghun defeated Darya Khan near Thatta in 1520, partitioned Sindh, and retained Firuz as a subordinate. Shah Hasan later expelled him, completing a phased ending usually placed around 1524.

sections.title: Read the exact id, map, and dates carefully

items.text: The live record is exact id sind, named Sind and indexed only from 1492 to 1500 with approximate dates. Its imported summary describes the modern Pakistani province. Coverage instead labels the record a state, with no reviewed card, override, or staged draft before this packet.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. Exact id sind appears once, in 1492, as one Polygon with one component, one ring, forty-nine positions, and precision one. Its bounding box runs roughly 59.982 to 72.816 degrees east and 23.489 to 31.384 degrees north.

The polygon contains sampled Thatta, Makli, Banbhore, Karachi, Hyderabad, Sehwan, Larkana, Sukkur, Rohri, and Multan. It excludes Umerkot, Nagarparkar, Bhuj, Jaisalmer, Bhakkar, Lahore, Ahmedabad, Kandahar, and Hormuz. Including Multan while omitting eastern Sindh makes its coarse atlas logic impossible to miss.

The target shares one TopoJSON arc apiece with atlas layers for the White Sheep Turks, Timurid Emirates, Rajastan, Gujarat, and Punjab. No polygon-overlap candidate or representative-point ownership overlap appears. Shared drawing seams help audit construction; they do not prove surveyed international borders.

The exact layer appears between 1400 and 1492, then disappears in 1500 although Samma government continued. Separate ids named sind-1783 and sindh-1800 appear centuries later. The card therefore corrects this record only and never merges every historical government that happened to rule a region called Sindh.

sections.title: Rule through commanders, chiefs, faith, and negotiation

items.text: Royal authority depended on commanders and regional notables. Darya Khan served Jam Nizamuddin as an administrator and military leader, oversaw water works, and later defended the dynasty. Calling him simply a general misses how warfare, cultivation, revenue, estates, and court guardianship were bundled together.

Sufi teachers and institutions mattered to Samma legitimacy. The large brick Jamia Masjid stood beside Shaikh Hammad Jamalis khanqah, and tradition credits Jam Tamachi with its patronage. Mosque, lodge, cemetery, and court formed overlapping social spaces rather than tidy modern departments of religion and government.

The long reign of Jam Nizamuddin is often remembered as a golden age, but praise in later chronicles must be tested. His surviving tomb, irrigation traditions, educational patronage, and coin-linked chronology provide firmer anchors. Prosperity was real for some people without becoming a universal medieval happiness survey.

Makli carving has clear Gujarat-linked features, and the official inventory suggests craftsmen may have come from Gujarat or Ahmedabad. Those artistic ties crossed todays border. The evidence secures exchange in skills; it does not reveal every artisans motives, workshop tenure, family route, or everyday language.

In the early sixteenth century, Central Asian changes pushed the Arghuns from Kandahar toward Sibi and Sindh. Their conquest was therefore both local and transregional. Jam Firuzs court divisions opened doors, but Babur, the Uzbeks, Safavids, and displaced Timurid elites shaped who arrived outside them.

sections.title: Farm, move water, fish, herd, and feed households

items.text: Agriculture and commerce were leading occupations in Samma Sindh. A study credits Darya Khan and minister Chagla with excavating the Saavi canal near Sehwan and records a large dam south of Manchar Lake. Such works linked royal revenue to the daily labor of diggers, irrigators, and cultivators.

Historical irrigation research describes river channels, inundation canals, deep wells, and water-lifting devices in Sindh. Water levels did not politely rise to every field, so people lifted them. The machinery may sound humble beside a tomb, but a working wheel could matter more to dinner than a carved balcony.

Period crop reconstructions include rice in suitable watered zones, millet and sorghum in drier lands, cotton and sugarcane in lift-irrigated areas, and wheat, barley, oilseeds, peas, and beans in riverine fields. They indicate possible ingredients and fibers, not one standard meal served across every household.

Fishing communities around Keenjhar Lake entered the Nuri and Jam Tamachi tradition, linking boats, fish, caste, court, and tax memory. The romance is later literature, not a wage ledger. It still preserves a social truth that lake laborers belonged to the political imagination of Samma Sindh.

Keenjhar still supports fishing livelihoods and remarkable aquatic diversity, which helps children picture why a lake mattered. Modern counts and water systems cannot be pushed backward five centuries. The safe fun fact is continuity of a working wetland landscape, not that a Samma fisher caught todays recorded species list.

sections.title: Trade by river, road, caravan, and sea

items.text: Fifteenth-century documents place Bhatia merchants from Thatta in Muscat, where they maintained an overseas colony and intense commercial links with lower Sindh. A merchant household could therefore have relatives, partners, credit, and news across the Arabian Sea long before European companies dominated those waters.

Sindh joined a larger Indian Ocean world of Hindu and Muslim merchant communities that kept ties to home while operating abroad. Trust moved through kinship, reputation, partnership, and correspondence. Ships carried goods, but networks carried the information needed to decide whose cargo and promise were believable.

The Indus connected inland cultivation and towns to the delta, while roads led toward Gujarat, Multan, Makran, and Kandahar. Political borders changed faster than commercial geography. Traders still faced tolls, raids, river shifts, and rulers, so calling Thatta connected should never be mistaken for calling travel easy.

Cotton, food crops, livestock products, stone, books, and crafted goods required different workers and routes. Surviving sources illuminate merchants and patrons better than porters, sailors, spinners, drovers, or market sellers. The economy depended on many people whose names never reached a royal chronicle.

Thatta trade survived beyond the Sammas, but later fame should not be pasted wholesale onto their period. The securely period-specific clue is the fifteenth-century Muscat connection. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Portuguese reports can explain later growth, yet they cannot automatically supply a 1492 shopping list.

sections.title: Meet families, women, children, and social differences

items.text: Royal genealogy records sons, rivals, marriages, guardianship, and succession because power traveled through families. It tells far less about ordinary households. A dynastic family tree can reveal political kinship, but it cannot stand in for how cultivators, fishers, artisans, enslaved people, or migrants organized care.

Nuri, remembered as a fisherwoman who married Jam Tamachi, became a powerful later symbol of humility, class difference, and loyalty to her people. Historians should distinguish the social memory from verified biography. Folklore can reveal what later Sindhis debated even when it cannot record palace dialogue.

An official monument inventory reports competing traditions for whether Nuri and Tamachi were buried at Keenjhar or Makli, and even questions later physical claims. That disagreement is useful evidence. Heritage is sometimes a family argument in stone, with archaeologists checking whether the relatives remembered the address correctly.

A dressed-stone pavilion at Makli is associated with Jam Tamachi, Queen Nuri, and a child. Its family grouping is suggestive, but attribution is not a household photograph. The monument supports remembrance of royal kinship while leaving childbirth, childcare, inheritance among commoners, and domestic work mostly undocumented.

Women appear in royal marriage, burial, poetry, and fisher-community memory, yet administrative voices overwhelmingly privilege elite men. Children appear even more rarely outside genealogy and educational tradition. This silence should stay visible: absence from court writing measures archival power, not absence from work, affection, grief, or play.

sections.title: Learn in mosques, madrasas, lodges, and scholarly families

items.text: Thatta, Sehwan, Bakhar, Nasarpur, Hala, and other towns supported religious learning. An Institute of Sindhology history describes Samma rulers funding buildings and stipends for scholars and students. Its spectacular claim of roughly one thousand Thatta madrasas comes from later tradition, not a contemporary enrollment census.

Early curricula emphasized Quranic commentary, hadith, Arabic grammar, and law; accounts of Nizamuddins reign add logic, philosophy, rational sciences, and medicine. Actual study differed by teacher and text. A curriculum list shows intellectual range, but not that every child attended or completed the same educational ladder.

The Jamia Masjid and nearby Hammad Jamali khanqah show how worship, teaching, lodging, patronage, and burial could cluster. Students learned through teachers, recitation, memorization, commentary, and manuscripts. The surviving brick structure identifies a setting, while desks, homework schedules, and report cards remain cheerfully absent.

A Thatta heritage record preserves a tradition that Shah Murad studied at a madrasa attached to Masjid Wali-i-Nimat during the later Samma period. Dates and locations remain debated. It offers a plausible neighborhood learning site, strongest when presented as documented tradition rather than excavated classroom certainty.

Around 1512, Makhdum Abhari migrated from Herat to Sindh and settled near Sehwan, where Darya Khans estate had become a learning center. He wrote commentaries, taught sons and pupils, and worked in rational and hadith sciences. Scholarship moved with refugees as well as royal invitations.

sections.title: Write in Arabic, Persian, and Sindhi, then read one sample

items.text: Persian served courtly and historical writing, Arabic carried scripture and learned disciplines, and Sindhi lived in speech, song, and developing literary forms. The boundaries were porous: scholars traveled, translated, commented, and composed across languages. No evidence supports imagining a neatly monolingual Samma bureaucracy or population.

Surviving accounts name Samma-period poets including Jam Juna, Hammad Jamali, Isa Langoti, and Jam Nindo in Persian literary history. Attribution is uneven, and few ordinary voices survive. Court and Sufi poetry can show ideals and networks more readily than conversations heard in fields or kitchens.

Written-language sample: السلطان نظام الدين شاه. Read right to left and romanized al-Sultan Nizam al-Din Shah, it means Sultan Nizam al-Din Shah. A peer-reviewed numismatic study quotes this phrase from the dated inscription at Jam Nizamuddins tomb. It is secure monumental titulature, not reconstructed everyday speech.

Coins of Jam Firuz and Jam Salah al-Din help reconstruct names, claims, and genealogy precisely because chronicles conflict. Metal carried writing through markets and taxes, although many users may have recognized weight or design without reading every title. Literacy and participation in a written economy were not identical.

The earliest full Persian history of Sindh, Tarikh-i Masumi, was completed around 1600, after the Sammas. It remains essential but retrospective. Scholars compare its narrative with inscriptions, monuments, and coins, a reminder that elegant prose written later does not automatically outrank stubborn evidence carved earlier.

sections.title: Build, carve, worship, mourn, and remember at Makli

items.text: Makli contains about half a million tombs and graves across roughly ten square kilometers, accumulated from the fourteenth through eighteenth centuries. Kings, queens, governors, saints, scholars, and philosophers appear there. The giant total belongs to the whole multi-dynasty cemetery, not to Samma construction alone.

Jam Nizamuddins square stone tomb carries twelve decorative bands with geometric forms, flowers, Quranic inscriptions, balconies, and fine calligraphy. Its dome was never completed. That unfinished roof is a wonderful historical antidote to the idea that every famous monument emerged exactly as an architect first imagined.

Craftspeople fused local practice with Gujarat-linked carving and wider Persian and Asian forms. UNESCO emphasizes adaptation into a distinctive local style rather than passive copying. Stonecutters, brickmakers, tile workers, calligraphers, laborers, and patrons together created the visual achievement now simplified under a rulers name.

The Makli monuments preserve political and social memory, but weather, salt, rain, earthquakes, riverbed movement, vandalism, and repair have changed them. Conservation records therefore belong to interpretation. What visitors see is authentic surviving fabric mixed with loss, stabilization, reconstruction decisions, and a great deal of patient paperwork.

Archaeological study warns that names assigned to tombs can rest on later chronicles, local tradition, location, style, or inscription, with unequal certainty. A beautiful building is not automatically a labeled biography. The safest card tells children both what experts identify and how strongly the stone itself agrees.

sections.title: Ask about health, water, houses, waste, and toilets honestly

items.text: An education history says medicine, or tib, entered advanced madrasa study during Nizamuddins reign. That supports learned medical knowledge in Samma Sindh, but not a public hospital system. The reviewed sources do not give reliable patient totals, clinic plans, fees, or equal access across town and countryside.

Across neighboring Indo-Muslim courts, physicians combined Islamicate textual medicine with experience of Indic drugs and treatments. This supplies regional context, not a prescription from Thatta. Without a Samma patients case record, the card will not claim which healer treated fever, childbirth, broken bones, or toothache.

River branches, canals, wells, dams, and water lifts supported farms and settlements, while the Indus could also shift course or flood. Water management demanded repeated communal labor. No king could issue one canal order and retire forever; silt, breaches, ropes, animals, and thirsty crops kept scheduling follow-up meetings.

Detailed Samma monument records describe mosques, tombs, a khanqah, stone, brick, lime, carving, and inscriptions, but they do not securely reconstruct ordinary houses. Room use, cooking spaces, bedding, household wells, privacy, and neighborhood density therefore remain important questions rather than opportunities for decorative invention.

Toilet answer: none of the reviewed Samma sources securely identifies a household latrine, cesspit, sewer network, or waste-collection service. People obviously managed bodily waste somehow, but the method, access, smell, and maintenance are undocumented here. Archaeological silence is less funny than a fake medieval flush toilet.

sections.title: Measure achievements, conquest, endings, and continuities

items.text: Samma achievement joined political survival, irrigation, cultivation, trade, scholarship, religious patronage, and local architectural invention. None depended on rulers alone. Canal diggers, cultivators, fishers, merchants, teachers, students, masons, carvers, boat crews, household workers, and unnamed taxpayers supplied the labor behind the golden-age label.

Darya Khans forces had resisted Arghun pressure under Nizamuddin, but factional conflict after 1508 weakened the court. Jam Firuz and Jam Salah al-Din competed, while displaced Arghuns sought a new base. The ending came from intersecting succession, frontier, and Central Asian pressures rather than one sudden bad decision.

Shah Beg Arghun defeated the Samma army near Thatta in December 1520; Darya Khan died fighting. Firuz submitted and retained lower Sindh temporarily while the conqueror held the rest. Partition means 1520 was a decisive rupture, but it was not yet the clean disappearance suggested by a single conquest date.

After Shah Begs death, Shah Hasan ended Firuzs subordinate rule and drove him toward Gujarat, completing the Samma political dissolution around 1524. Firuz later tried unsuccessfully to recover the throne. The dynasty ended as government; Sindhi communities, farms, learning, stories, and craft traditions did not evaporate.

The atlas removes exact id sind in 1500, roughly two decades before the historical ending, then creates other Sind records centuries later. That software seam is useful navigation, not destiny. The card closes with Arghun takeover around 1524 and leaves Kalhora, Talpur, British, and modern Sindh histories to their own records.

ending.text: The Samma ending unfolded in stages. Shah Beg Arghun defeated Darya Khan and Jam Firuz near Thatta in December 1520, divided Sindh, and left Firuz governing a reduced southern share. After Shah Beg died, Shah Hasan removed that subordinate arrangement and expelled Firuz toward Gujarat, completing the dynastys loss of government around 1524. Firuz later attempted a return but did not restore Samma rule. The outcome was conquest and political dissolution, not the disappearance of Sindhi people, irrigation, trade, fishing, scholarship, Sufi institutions, or Makli craft. The exact atlas layer vanishes in 1500, so its software endpoint is about two decades too early and must never be narrated as the fall.
